def-tdmath-extended-convex-function:
## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. Write $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with its usual order and extended addition; in a convex combination set $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ and $\lambda\cdot(+\infty)=+\infty$ for $\lambda>0$. A function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **proper** when it never takes the value $-\infty$ and its effective domain

$$\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:f(x)<+\infty\}$$

is nonempty. It is **convex** when

$$f((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d,\ t\in[0,1]).$$

It is **lower semicontinuous** when each weak sublevel set $\{x:f(x)\le a\}$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, for every $a\in\mathbb R$. Its **epigraph** is

$$\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.$$

On this page “closed proper convex” means proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous in these conventions. The pairing of $p,x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the Euclidean inner product $\langle p,x\rangle$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgrad:
## Definition

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is $f^*:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,

$$f^*(p):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).$$

The supremum is taken in $\overline{\mathbb R}$; its defining set is nonempty and consists of real numbers, so $f^*(p)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. The **biconjugate** is an extended-real expression that may also take $-\infty$ when its defining supremum is over the empty set:

$$f^{**}(x):=\sup_{\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f^*(p)<+\infty\}}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\bigr),$$

with the convention $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the **subdifferential** is

$$\partial f(x):=\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in\mathbb R^d\};$$

set $\partial f(x)=\varnothing$ for $x\notin\operatorname{dom}f$. A vector in $\partial f(x)$ is a subgradient at $x$. All pairings use [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equi:
## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ use the conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Then $f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, and $f$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed.
lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation:
## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.
lem-tdmath-fenchel-young-equality:
## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper, let $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $f^*(p)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$. Equality holds exactly when $p\in\partial f(x)$, equivalently when $x$ attains the supremum defining $f^*(p)$; in that case the supremum is finite.
thm-tdmath-finite-dimensional-biconjugat:
## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. With the Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate of [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]], one has

$$f^{**}(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$
thm-tdmath-fenchel-attainment:
## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex, let $p\in\mathbb R^d$, and define $g(x)=f(x)-\langle p,x\rangle$. Assume $g$ is **coercive**, meaning that for every $M\in\mathbb R$ there is $R>0$ such that $\|x\|_2\ge R$ implies $g(x)>M$. Then $g$ has a finite global minimum at some $x_*\in\operatorname{dom}f$. The supremum defining $f^*(p)$ is finite and attained at $x_*$, and $p\in\partial f(x_*)$. No uniqueness is asserted.
thm-tdmath-finite-mixture-envelope:
## Statement

Let $m\ge1$, let $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$. Put

$$\Delta_m=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^m:\theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1\},\qquad P=\operatorname{conv}\{q_1,\ldots,q_m\}.$$

For $x\in P$ let $\Theta_x=\{\theta\in\Delta_m:\sum_i\theta_iq_i=x\}$ and define

$$f_{\rm mix}(x)=\min_{\theta\in\Theta_x}\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i a_i;$$

set $f_{\rm mix}(x)=+\infty$ for $x\notin P$. Then every minimum is attained; $f_{\rm mix}$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; and it is the greatest convex extended-real function satisfying $f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le a_i$ for every $i$. Consequently $f_{\rm mix}=f_{\rm mix}^{**}$. If $p\in\partial f_{\rm mix}(x)$ and $\theta$ is any minimizing mixture for $x$, then every $i$ with $\theta_i>0$ satisfies

$$a_i=\langle p,q_i\rangle-f_{\rm mix}^*(p).$$

Thus all occupied data points $(q_i,a_i)$ lie on one supporting affine hyperplane. The assertion is finite-dimensional and makes no claim about infinite families.
cor-tdmath-ordered-finite-mixture-envelo:
## Statement

Assume the strict-reference representation conclusion of the draft supplier [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] for its nonempty state set $X$ and stated comparison hypotheses. For a finite nonempty list of distinct states $s_1,\ldots,s_m\in X$, let $e_s$ be the unit-state compound defined in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]; it is a mass-one point mass by [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]. For $\theta\in\Delta_m$, put $M_\theta=\sum_i\theta_i e_{s_i}$ and set $V(\theta):=\sum_i\theta_iS(s_i)$. Suppose a coordinate assignment $\chi$ on these compounds satisfies $\chi(M_\theta)=\sum_i\theta_iq_i$ for fixed $q_i\in\mathbb R^d$. For each $x$, define the value to be $+\infty$ if no $\theta\in\Delta_m$ has coordinate $x$. Then the minimum represented value among those finite mixtures, with that empty-feasible-set convention, is exactly the finite-mixture envelope $f_{\rm mix}(x)$ of [[thm-tdmath-finite-mixture-envelope]], with all its attainment, convexity, lower-semicontinuity, biconjugation, and supporting-face conclusions. This is the complete conditional transfer under the representation conclusion and affine coordinate assignment; the supplier definition and mass-one fact are provided locally.
lem-tdmath-lever-rule:
## Statement

Let $v_a,v_b\in\mathbb R$ with $v_a<v_b$. A fraction $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfies $v=(1-\lambda)v_a+\lambda v_b$ exactly when $v\in[v_a,v_b]$ and

$$\lambda=\frac{v-v_a}{v_b-v_a}.$$

This fraction is unique. At $v=v_a$ it is $0$, and at $v=v_b$ it is $1$; no admissible fraction gives a value outside the endpoint interval.
lem-tdmath-concave-affine-maximizer-and-:
## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. For $x,y\in U$, suppose the whole segment $[x,y]$ lies in $U$ and its concavity inequality holds:

$$f(x+t(y-x))\ge(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad(0\le t\le1).$$

Then the supporting bound is $f(y)\le f(x)+Df(x)(y-x)$. In particular this bound holds for every $x,y$ in any convex subset of $U$ on which $f$ is concave. No global convexity of $U$ is assumed.

Let $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ be linear, $b\in\mathbb R^k$, and $F=U\cap\{x:Ax=b\}$. Suppose $x_*\in F$, $Df(x_*)h=0$ for every $h\in\ker A$, and for every $y\in F$ the segment $[x_*,y]$ lies in $U$ and has the displayed concavity inequality. Then $x_*$ is a global maximum of $f$ on $F$. If $F$ is convex and $f|_F$ is strictly concave, meaning the inequality is strict for distinct endpoints and $0<t<1$, the maximum is unique.

For the curvature clause, suppose $f\in C^2(U)$ and fix $x\in U$. If, for every $h\in\mathbb R^d$, all sufficiently small $|t|$ satisfy $x\pm th\in U$ and

$$f(x+th)+f(x-th)\le2f(x),$$

then the Hessian bilinear form $D^2f(x)=D(Df)(x)$ satisfies $D^2f(x)[h,h]\le0$ for every $h$. This condition holds whenever $f$ is concave on a neighborhood of $x$. Thus a $C^2$ function concave on an open convex region has negative-semidefinite Hessian there. Concavity alone does not assert strict curvature.
lem-tdmath-constrained-curvature:
## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ be linear, let $b\in\mathbb R^k$, and let $x_*\in U$ satisfy $Ax_*=b$. Put $T=\ker A$. Assume $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable and has second directional derivatives represented by a continuous matrix field: there is a continuous map $H:U\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with symmetric values, and for every $x\in U$ and $h\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}f(x+th)\right|_{t=0}=Q_x(h):=h^{\mathsf T}H(x)h.$$

Assume stationarity $Df(x_*)h=0$ for every $h\in T$. If $Q_{x_*}(h_0)<0$ for some $h_0\in T$, then $x_*$ is not a local minimum of $f$ on $\{x\in U:Ax=b\}$. If $Q_{x_*}(h)>0$ for every nonzero $h\in T$, then $x_*$ is a strict local minimum on that feasible slice. If $T=\{0\}$, the latter conclusion holds because $x_*$ is the only feasible point.
lem-tdmath-stoichiometric-tangent-cone:
## Statement

Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. If a potential $\Phi$ is differentiable on an open neighborhood of the relevant amounts and $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$, define $\mu_j=\partial\Phi/\partial n_j$; then

$$Df(\xi_*)h=\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h.$$

The tangent-cone and optimality claims are mathematical deductions. They do not assert that a particular physical system obeys this model or is at equilibrium.
thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank:
## Statement

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.
thm-tdmath-phase-dimension:
## Statement

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.
